Central difference stencils become unstable for singular perturbation problems with boundary layers unless mesh graded clustering is applied.
Extending to higher-order stencils (e.g. 5-point O(h⁴) stencil for y'') requires special asymmetric stencils near boundaries to prevent underdetermined systems.

title: Heat Equation Parabolic PDE: Crank-Nicolson Unconditional Stability
subject: mathematics
aim: Implement the implicit Crank-Nicolson scheme for the one-dimensional unsteady heat conduction PDE ∂u/∂t = α ∂²u/∂x², demonstrate unconditional numerical stability, and verify second-order temporal and spatial convergence O(Δt² + Δx²).
settings: Parabolic PDE manifold: ∂u/∂t = ∂²u/∂x² on x ∈ [0, π], t ∈ [0, 0.5] with Dirichlet boundaries u(0, t) = u(π, t) = 0
Analytic thermal solution: Fundamental Fourier mode u(x, t) = exp(-t) · sin(x)
Crank-Nicolson stencil: (u_i^{n+1} - u_i^n)/Δt = 0.5 [δ_x² u_i^{n+1} + δ_x² u_i^n] / Δx² (implicit trapezoidal time centering)
Mesh refinement coupling: Set diffusion Fourier number r = Δt / Δx² = 1.0 so Δt = Δx² or coupled halving h = Δx

apparatus.name: One-Dimensional Thermal Bar Grid
apparatus.purpose: Discretizes the continuous spatial domain [0, π] into N uniform sub-elements with node spacing Δx = π/N.

apparatus.name: Crank-Nicolson Matrix Assembler
apparatus.purpose: Assembles the tridiagonal system (I - 0.5 r δ_x²) u^{n+1} = (I + 0.5 r δ_x²) u^n where r = Δt / Δx².

apparatus.name: Thomas Tridiagonal Solver
apparatus.purpose: Inverts the strictly diagonally dominant implicit matrix at each time step in O(N) operations.

apparatus.name: Von Neumann Stability Analyzer
apparatus.purpose: Calculates the Fourier amplification factor G(k) = (1 - 2r sin²(kΔx/2)) / (1 + 2r sin²(kΔx/2)) showing |G| ≤ 1 for all r.

apparatus.name: Exact Fourier Mode Evaluator
apparatus.purpose: Computes exact decaying solution u(x, t) = e^{-t} sin(x) to evaluate exact spatial and temporal error fields.

apparatus.name: Log-Log Asymptotic Slope Engine
apparatus.purpose: Performs linear regression on (ln(h), ln(E_max)) to verify the theoretical second-order slope α = 2.000.

procedure.title: Define Parabolic Heat Diffusion Problem
procedure.text: Set up ∂u/∂t = ∂²u/∂x² on [0, π] with initial condition u(x, 0) = sin(x) and exact solution u(x, t) = e^{-t} sin(x).

procedure.title: Initialize Coupled Space-Time Mesh
procedure.text: For test levels k = 1 to 6, set spatial grid spacing h = Δx = 0.20 / 2^{k-1} and time step Δt proportional to h.

procedure.title: Formulate Crank-Nicolson Stencils
procedure.text: Construct tridiagonal matrices with diagonal 1 + r and off-diagonals -r/2 on the left, and diagonal 1 - r and off-diagonals r/2 on the right.

procedure.title: Execute Time Marching via TDMA
procedure.text: At each time step t_n → t_{n+1}, multiply current state by right matrix and solve tridiagonal system via the Thomas algorithm.

procedure.title: Measure Maximum Thermal Field Discrepancy
procedure.text: At final time t = 0.5, compute absolute errors |u(x_i, 0.5) - u_i^N| across all nodes and extract supremum error E_max.

procedure.title: Fit Second-Order Convergence Slope
procedure.text: Plot ln(E_max) versus ln(h) and compute the linear regression gradient to verify α = 2.000 with R² = 1.000000.

topics.question: Why is the explicit Forward Time Central Space (FTCS) scheme problematic for the heat equation?
topics.answer: FTCS has local error O(Δt + Δx²), but von Neumann stability analysis reveals that the amplification factor satisfies |G| ≤ 1 only when the diffusion number r = α Δt / Δx² ≤ 1/2. Halving Δx requires a 4-fold reduction in Δt, leading to astronomical numbers of tiny time steps on fine spatial meshes.

topics.question: How did John Crank and Phyllis Nicolson achieve unconditional stability in 1947?
topics.answer: Crank and Nicolson averaged the central difference spatial stencils at the current time level t_n and the future time level t_{n+1} (a trapezoidal rule in time). This symmetric time-centering cancels the leading first-order temporal error, achieving second-order accuracy O(Δt² + Δx²) while guaranteeing |G| ≤ 1 for any choice of r = Δt / Δx².

topics.question: How does von Neumann stability analysis prove Crank-Nicolson is unconditionally stable?
topics.answer: Substituting the discrete Fourier mode u_j^n = G^n e^{i k j Δx} into the Crank-Nicolson stencil yields G = [1 - 2r sin²(θ/2)] / [1 + 2r sin²(θ/2)], where θ = k Δx. Since the denominator is always greater than or equal to the absolute value of the numerator for any r > 0, |G| ≤ 1 holds unconditionally for all wavenumbers k.

topics.question: What is the computational cost of inverting the Crank-Nicolson matrix at each time step?
topics.answer: In one spatial dimension, the implicit matrix is tridiagonal and strictly diagonally dominant. The Thomas algorithm inverts it in exactly O(N) operations per time step, meaning the implicit step is essentially as fast as an explicit step while permitting time steps orders of magnitude larger.

topics.question: Can the Crank-Nicolson scheme produce spurious numerical oscillations even though it is stable?
topics.answer: Yes. When r = Δt / Δx² ≫ 1, the amplification factor for the highest spatial frequency (θ = π) approaches G ≈ -1. While bounded (|G| ≤ 1), the negative sign causes high-frequency components to oscillate sign from step to step instead of decaying monotonically, requiring spatial smoothing or L-stable implicit methods (BDF2 or backward Euler).

topics.question: How is Crank-Nicolson extended to two spatial dimensions (2D heat equation)?
topics.answer: In 2D, the direct implicit matrix is no longer tridiagonal but pentadiagonal with large bandwidth, making direct inversion O(N³) expensive. The Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) method of Peaceman and Rachford splits each time step into two half-steps, inverting tridiagonal systems along x then y, restoring O(N) efficiency.

topics.question: What is the physical interpretation of the heat equation as a dissipative system?
topics.answer: The heat equation represents diffusive thermal equilibration driven by Fourier's law of conduction. As t → ∞, all high-frequency spatial temperature gradients decay exponentially as e^{-k² t}, smoothing any initial discontinuity and dissipating total thermodynamic entropy into uniform equilibrium.

quiz.question: What is the stability restriction on the diffusion number r = α Δt / Δx² for the Crank-Nicolson scheme?
quiz.explanation: Crank-Nicolson is unconditionally stable by von Neumann analysis: its amplification factor satisfies |G| ≤ 1 for all r > 0.

quiz.question: What is the theoretical order of accuracy of the Crank-Nicolson scheme in time and space?
quiz.explanation: Because of symmetric time-centering at t_{n+1/2}, Crank-Nicolson achieves second-order accuracy in both time and space: O(Δt² + Δx²).

quiz.question: What computational algorithm enables the 1D implicit Crank-Nicolson step to be solved in linear O(N) time?
quiz.explanation: The implicit Crank-Nicolson matrix is tridiagonal and strictly diagonally dominant, allowing the Thomas algorithm to invert it in O(N) time.

quiz.question: What undesirable numerical artifact can occur in Crank-Nicolson when the grid parameter r = Δt / Δx² is chosen extremely large?
options: Node-to-node sign oscillations for high-frequency components (G ≈ -1)
Division by zero in the Thomas algorithm
quiz.explanation: For very large r, the amplification factor G for high-frequency modes approaches -1, causing bounded but non-physical spurious oscillations.

intro: The mathematical modeling of diffusive transport—from transient thermal conduction in aerospace heat shields to chemical solute dispersion and financial option pricing via the Black-Scholes PDE—is governed by parabolic partial differential equations. Discretizing the heat equation ∂u/∂t = α ∂²u/∂x² with explicit forward differences leads to severe numerical instability: the time step must satisfy the crippling Courant-type condition r = α Δt / Δx² ≤ 1/2, forcing billions of tiny time steps on fine meshes. In 1947, British mathematicians John Crank and Phyllis Nicolson devised an elegant implicit formulation that averages spatial derivatives at time levels n and n + 1. By centering the stencil at t_{n+1/2}, Crank-Nicolson achieves unconditional von Neumann stability (|G| ≤ 1 for all r) and second-order accuracy O(Δt² + Δx²). In this laboratory, we implement the Crank-Nicolson scheme, invert the tridiagonal system via the Thomas algorithm, and verify the second-order O(h²) error convergence.
modelExtra: The simulation executes the implicit Crank-Nicolson scheme across coupled mesh spacings h = 0.20 / 2^{k-1} on the thermal diffusion PDE ∂u/∂t = ∂²u/∂x². The maximum error is measured against the exact fundamental Fourier mode u(x, t) = e^{-t} sin(x). The logarithmic regression ln(E) = α·ln(h) + ln(C) extracts the asymptotic order α = 2.000 with R² = 1.000000.
precautions: Verify that the tridiagonal matrix diagonal 1 + r strictly exceeds off-diagonal sums to preserve strict diagonal dominance in the Thomas algorithm.
Incorporate Dirichlet boundary values into the right-hand vector to prevent artificial boundary reflection errors.
Be cautious of very large diffusion numbers r > 10 when initial data has sharp discontinuities, as G ≈ -1 can induce spurious oscillations.
Ensure floating point precision remains 64-bit IEEE 754 to prevent roundoff accumulation across hundreds of implicit time steps.
Verify that spatial node count N and time step count M are updated consistently to maintain the chosen scaling relation r = Δt / Δx².
For non-linear thermal conductivity α(u), solve the resulting non-linear tridiagonal system using Picard or Newton-Raphson iteration.
limitations: While Crank-Nicolson is A-stable, it is not L-stable: it does not damp stiff high-frequency error components as rapidly as backward Euler or BDF2.
In 2D and 3D, direct Crank-Nicolson produces banded matrices with large bandwidth, requiring Alternating Direction Implicit (ADI) split solvers.
Crank-Nicolson cannot handle hyperbolic wave propagation without introducing severe dispersion and phase errors.

title: Wave Equation Hyperbolic PDE & Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) Stability
subject: mathematics
aim: Implement the explicit leapfrog finite difference scheme for the one-dimensional hyperbolic wave equation ∂²u/∂t² = c² ∂²u/∂x², evaluate acoustic wave propagation and phase velocity dispersion, and quantitatively verify the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) stability criterion C = c Δt / Δx ≤ 1.000.
settings: Hyperbolic wave equation: ∂²u/∂t² = c² ∂²u/∂x² with wave speed c = 1.0 on x ∈ [0, 2] with fixed ends u(0, t) = u(2, t) = 0
Explicit leapfrog stencil: u_i^{n+1} = 2 u_i^n - u_i^{n-1} + C² [u_{i+1}^n - 2 u_i^n + u_{i-1}^n] where C = c Δt / Δx
CFL stability limit: Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy condition strictly mandates C ≤ 1.000 for non-growing bounded oscillations
Initial pulse profile: Plucked string Gaussian profile u(x, 0) = exp(-100 (x - 1.0)²) with zero initial velocity ∂u/∂t(x, 0) = 0

apparatus.name: One-Dimensional Acoustic Grid
apparatus.purpose: Discretizes the spatial wave domain into N cells with node spacing Δx and time increments Δt.

apparatus.name: Explicit Leapfrog Wave Stepper
apparatus.purpose: Marches wave state across three consecutive time levels: past u^{n-1}, present u^n, and future u^{n+1}.

apparatus.name: Initial Velocity Ghost Stepper
apparatus.purpose: Applies special initial step u_i¹ = u_i⁰ + 0.5 C² [u_{i+1}⁰ - 2 u_i⁰ + u_{i-1}⁰] enforcing ∂u/∂t = 0 with O(Δt²) precision.

apparatus.name: Von Neumann Characteristic Analyzer
apparatus.purpose: Computes amplification roots λ = (1 - 2 C² sin²(θ/2)) ± i √(1 - (1 - 2 C² sin²(θ/2))²), proving |λ| = 1 if C ≤ 1.

apparatus.name: Numerical Dispersion Scanner
apparatus.purpose: Measures numerical phase velocity c_num(k) / c = (2 / (C k Δx)) arcsin(C sin(k Δx / 2)) showing parasitic pulse distortion.

apparatus.name: CFL Threshold Verifier
apparatus.purpose: Monitors energy growth to empirically determine the critical stability threshold C_cfl = 1.000.

procedure.title: Initialize Wave Domain & Gaussian Pulse
procedure.text: Set up wave speed c = 1.0 on [0, 2] with fixed boundary conditions u(0, t) = u(2, t) = 0 and initial pulse u(x, 0) = e^{-100(x-1)²}.

procedure.title: Configure Courant Numbers
procedure.text: Set up standardized Courant parameters C = c Δt / Δx across settings k = 1 to 6 approaching the stability limit C = 1.000.

procedure.title: Execute Second-Order Time Starter
procedure.text: Compute time level n = 1 using the Taylor expansion u¹ = u⁰ + (C²/2) δ_x² u⁰ satisfying zero initial velocity ∂u/∂t = 0.

procedure.title: March Wave Leapfrog Stencil
procedure.text: Compute u^{n+1} = 2 u^n - u^{n-1} + C² δ_x² u^n, observing pulse splitting into left- and right-propagating d'Alembert wave packets.

procedure.title: Analyze Stability Transition
procedure.text: Confirm that for C ≤ 1.000 the total wave energy remains bounded and conserved, while for C > 1.000 the solution suffers explosive exponential instability.

procedure.title: Fit Standardized CFL Metric
procedure.text: Log the standardized wavefront metric across settings k = 1 to 6 and perform linear regression to confirm the critical parameter C_cfl = 1.000.

topics.question: What is the physical interpretation of the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition?
topics.answer: The CFL condition states that the numerical domain of dependence of a finite difference scheme must contain the physical domain of dependence of the underlying hyperbolic PDE. If C = c Δt / Δx > 1, the physical characteristic lines travel faster than numerical information can propagate across the grid, rendering the numerical scheme fundamentally blind to physical wave signals and causing catastrophic instability.

topics.question: How does d'Alembert's formula represent the exact solution to the 1D wave equation?
topics.answer: Jean le Rond d'Alembert proved in 1747 that the general solution to ∂²u/∂t² = c² ∂²u/∂x² is u(x, t) = f(x - ct) + g(x + ct), representing two non-dispersive wave packets propagating in opposite directions at constant velocity c without changing shape.

topics.question: What is the amplification factor of the leapfrog wave scheme under von Neumann analysis?
topics.answer: The amplification factor satisfies the quadratic equation λ² - 2 (1 - 2 C² sin²(θ/2)) λ + 1 = 0. When C ≤ 1, the discriminant is non-positive, yielding complex conjugate roots with magnitude |λ| = 1 identically. This means the scheme is neutrally stable (non-dissipative) and conserves energy for C ≤ 1.

topics.question: What happens when the Courant number equals exactly C = 1.0?
topics.answer: When C = c Δt / Δx = 1.0, the numerical scheme becomes mathematically exact: numerical grid characteristics coincide perfectly with physical characteristics, eliminating all numerical dispersion and transporting wave packets with zero distortion.

topics.question: What is numerical dispersion in wave simulations?
topics.answer: When C < 1, the numerical phase velocity c_{num}(k) depends on the spatial wavenumber k: high-frequency short waves propagate slower than physical speed c. Over long integration times, sharp wave fronts disperse into parasitic trailing ripples.

topics.question: How are non-reflecting boundary conditions (absorbing boundaries) formulated?
topics.answer: At open boundaries where waves should exit without reflecting back into the computational domain, one applies one-way wave equations (Engquist-Majda conditions) such as ∂u/∂t + c ∂u/∂x = 0 at the right boundary x = L, or surrounds the domain with a Perfectly Matched Layer (PML).

topics.question: Why is the wave equation called 'hyperbolic'?
topics.answer: Classified by the discriminant B² - 4AC of general second-order PDEs A u_{xx} + B u_{xt} + C u_{tt} + ... = 0, the wave equation has A = -c², B = 0, C = 1, so B² - 4AC = 4c² > 0. A positive discriminant defines hyperbolic PDEs, which are characterized by finite propagation speeds along real characteristic curves.

quiz.question: What is the maximum Courant number C = c Δt / Δx for which the explicit leapfrog wave equation scheme is stable?
quiz.explanation: The Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition requires C = c Δt / Δx ≤ 1.0 to ensure the numerical domain of dependence covers the physical domain.

quiz.question: What remarkable behavior occurs when the leapfrog wave scheme is executed at exactly C = 1.0?
options: The numerical solution is exact with zero dispersion error
quiz.explanation: At C = 1.0, grid characteristics match the physical characteristic curves x ± ct = constant exactly, eliminating all numerical dispersion.

quiz.question: What mathematical magnitude do the amplification roots |λ| have when C ≤ 1 in the leapfrog wave scheme?
quiz.explanation: Because the product of the quadratic roots is 1 and the discriminant is negative for C ≤ 1, both roots lie on the unit circle (|λ| = 1), conserving wave energy.

quiz.question: What causes sharp initial wave pulses to develop trailing ripples when integrated with C < 1?
options: Numerical dispersion (different wavenumbers travel at different numerical phase speeds)
quiz.explanation: Numerical dispersion causes short-wavelength Fourier components to travel slower than the true speed of sound c, creating trailing oscillations.

intro: From acoustic sound propagation and seismic earthquake waves to electromagnetic radiation and gravitational ripples in spacetime, dynamic non-dissipative transport is governed by hyperbolic partial differential equations. In 1928, Richard Courant, Kurt Friedrichs, and Hans Lewy published their landmark paper establishing the foundational stability principle of computational science: the Courant-Friedrichs-Lewy (CFL) condition. For explicit finite difference schemes, numerical information propagates at grid velocity Δx/Δt; if the physical wave speed c exceeds this numerical speed (Courant number C = c Δt / Δx > 1), physical domain characteristics escape the numerical domain of dependence, triggering instantaneous, violent exponential instability. In this computational laboratory, we implement the explicit leapfrog scheme for the 1D wave equation, simulate d'Alembert pulse splitting, investigate numerical dispersion, and verify the critical CFL stability parameter C = 1.000.
modelExtra: The simulation executes the explicit leapfrog wave scheme across standardized Courant settings k = 1 to 6. The standardized wave metric scales linearly with step index k, confirming the theoretical CFL stability limit C_cfl = 1.000 with R² = 1.000000.
precautions: Always verify that Courant number C = c Δt / Δx ≤ 1.000 before initiating time integration to prevent catastrophic numerical overflow.
Implement the initial velocity step using second-order Taylor expansion u¹ = u⁰ + (C²/2) δ_x² u⁰ to prevent degrading global accuracy to first order.
Ensure boundary conditions at fixed ends u(0, t) = u(L, t) = 0 are enforced at every time step to prevent boundary energy injection.
Verify that floating point precision remains 64-bit IEEE 754 during time-marching across thousands of wave periods.
When simulating open domains, implement absorbing boundary conditions to prevent artificial wave packet reflection from grid boundaries.
Monitor total discrete energy E^n = 0.5 ∑ [((u^{n+1} - u^{n-1})/(2Δt))² + c² ((u_{i+1}^n - u_i^n)/Δx)²] to detect instability onset.
limitations: Explicit leapfrog is strictly conditionally stable; in multi-dimensional domains, the CFL limit tightens to c Δt √(1/Δx² + 1/Δy²) ≤ 1.
Numerical dispersion distorts high-frequency wave packets over long distances, requiring spectral methods or high-order compact stencils.
The leapfrog scheme requires storage of three consecutive time levels, increasing memory footprint compared to two-level schemes.

title: Laplace and Poisson Elliptic PDEs: Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel & SOR Relaxation
subject: mathematics
aim: Discretize the two-dimensional Poisson equation ∇²u = f(x, y) using the 5-point central difference star stencil, analyze stationary iterative relaxation methods (Jacobi, Gauss-Seidel, Successive Over-Relaxation), and quantitatively determine the optimal relaxation parameter ω_opt = 1.729.
settings: Elliptic PDE manifold: 2D Poisson equation ∂²u/∂x² + ∂²u/∂y² = -2 π² sin(πx) sin(πy) on unit square Ω = [0, 1]²
5-point discrete Laplacian star: (u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4 u_{i,j}) / h² = f_{i,j}
Grid resolution: N × N interior mesh (N = 20) with uniform grid spacing h = 1.0 / (N + 1)
Theoretical optimal SOR parameter: ω_opt = 2 / (1 + √(1 - ρ_J²)) ≈ 1.729 where ρ_J = cos(π h) ≈ 0.9888

apparatus.name: Two-Dimensional Grid Allocator
apparatus.purpose: Allocates (N+2) × (N+2) potential matrix u(i, j) with boundary registers initialized to zero.

apparatus.name: 5-Point Laplacian Star Operator
apparatus.purpose: Evaluates discrete Laplacian (u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4 u_{i,j})/h².

apparatus.name: Jacobi Simultaneous Relaxer
apparatus.purpose: Updates new potential buffer u^{k+1} using only values from previous iteration u^k.

apparatus.name: Gauss-Seidel In-Place Relaxer
apparatus.purpose: Immediately overwrites potential values u_{i,j} in raster scan order, cutting iteration count in half.

apparatus.name: SOR Acceleration Engine
apparatus.purpose: Over-relaxes the correction: u_{i,j}^{k+1} = (1 - ω) u_{i,j}^k + (ω/4) [u_{i+1,j}^k + u_{i-1,j}^{k+1} + u_{i,j+1}^k + u_{i,j-1}^{k+1} - h² f_{i,j}].

apparatus.name: Optimal Parameter Analyzer
apparatus.purpose: Tracks spectral radius ρ(ω) to confirm minimum iteration count at the theoretical optimum ω_opt = 1.729.

procedure.title: Define 2D Poisson Test System
procedure.text: Set up ∇²u = -2 π² sin(πx) sin(πy) on [0, 1]² with homogeneous Dirichlet boundaries u = 0 and exact solution u = sin(πx) sin(πy).

procedure.title: Initialize Grid & Finite Difference Mesh
procedure.text: Allocate N = 20 interior grid points with uniform spacing h = 1/21, setting initial potential guess u_{i,j} = 0 everywhere.

procedure.title: Execute Jacobi and Gauss-Seidel Relaxations
procedure.text: Run baseline iterations to observe slow asymptotic convergence governed by spectral radii ρ_J ≈ 0.9888 and ρ_{GS} = ρ_J² ≈ 0.9778.

procedure.title: Apply Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR)
procedure.text: Vary relaxation factor ω from 1.0 to 1.95, measuring total iterations required to reduce residual norm below 10⁻⁶.

procedure.title: Identify Minimum Iteration Valley
procedure.text: Confirm that at ω_opt = 2 / (1 + sin(π h)) ≈ 1.729, iteration count drops from over 400 down to fewer than 35.

procedure.title: Record Linearized Optimal Metric
procedure.text: Log the standardized relaxation response across settings k = 1 to 6 and fit linear regression to confirm target ω_opt = 1.729.

topics.question: What is the physical interpretation of Laplace's and Poisson's equations?
topics.answer: Laplace's equation ∇²u = 0 models steady-state conservative potential fields in source-free media: electrostatic potentials, steady thermal equilibria, irrotational fluid velocity potentials, and gravitational fields. Poisson's equation ∇²u = f incorporates localized sources or charge distributions f(x, y).

topics.question: How is the 5-point discrete Laplacian stencil derived in two dimensions?
topics.answer: Applying second-order central difference approximations to both second partial derivatives yields ∂²u/∂x² ≈ (u_{i+1,j} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i-1,j})/h² and ∂²u/∂y² ≈ (u_{i,j+1} - 2u_{i,j} + u_{i,j-1})/h². Summing these gives the classic 5-point star: ∇²u ≈ (u_{i+1,j} + u_{i-1,j} + u_{i,j+1} + u_{i,j-1} - 4u_{i,j})/h² + O(h²).

topics.question: What is the mean value property of harmonic functions and how does it manifest in Jacobi relaxation?
topics.answer: Harmonic functions (solutions to ∇²u = 0) satisfy the Gauss Mean Value Theorem: the potential at any point equals the average of its values on any surrounding circle. In Jacobi relaxation for Laplace's equation, each interior grid point is updated simply as the arithmetic average of its four nearest neighbors: u_{i,j}^{k+1} = (u_{i+1,j}^k + u_{i-1,j}^k + u_{i,j+1}^k + u_{i,j-1}^k) / 4.

topics.question: How did David Young derive the formula for the optimal SOR relaxation parameter ω_opt?
topics.answer: In his 1950 doctoral dissertation, David Young proved that for matrices possessing 'Property A' (such as 5-point stencils with red-black ordering), the eigenvalues μ of the Jacobi iteration matrix and λ of the SOR iteration matrix satisfy (λ + ω - 1)² = ω² μ² λ. Minimizing the spectral radius max |λ| with respect to ω yields Young's celebrated formula: ω_opt = 2 / (1 + √(1 - ρ_J²)).

topics.question: What is the asymptotic convergence speedup of SOR over Gauss-Seidel for fine grids (h ≪ 1)?
topics.answer: For grid spacing h, the Jacobi spectral radius is ρ_J ≈ 1 - (π² h²)/2. Gauss-Seidel converges at rate -ln(ρ_{GS}) ≈ π² h², requiring O(N²) iterations. For optimal SOR, the spectral radius is ρ_{SOR} = ω_opt - 1 ≈ 1 - 2π h, requiring only O(N) iterations—an order of magnitude reduction in computational time.

topics.question: What is Red-Black (checkerboard) Gauss-Seidel ordering and why is it important?
topics.answer: Standard Gauss-Seidel updates nodes in raster-scan order, creating serial dependencies. Red-Black ordering colors grid points like a chessboard: all 'red' points depend only on 'black' points, and vice versa. This allows all red points to be updated simultaneously in parallel, followed by all black points, enabling vectorization on GPUs and multicore CPUs.

topics.question: Why are multigrid methods even faster than SOR for huge Poisson problems?
topics.answer: SOR relaxes local high-frequency error components quickly, but smooth, low-frequency error modes take thousands of iterations to propagate across the domain. Multigrid methods project residual errors onto a hierarchy of coarser grids where low frequencies appear high-frequency, solving the Poisson equation in optimal O(N) total operations.

quiz.question: What is the exact formula for the optimal Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR) parameter ω_opt in terms of the Jacobi spectral radius ρ_J?
quiz.explanation: David Young's formula proves that the spectral radius of the SOR iteration matrix is minimized when ω_opt = 2 / (1 + √(1 - ρ_J²)).

quiz.question: For a grid spacing h = 1/21 (N = 20 interior points), what is the approximate numerical value of the optimal SOR parameter ω_opt?
quiz.explanation: With ρ_J = cos(π/21) ≈ 0.9888, evaluating Young's formula yields ω_opt = 2 / (1 + √(1 - 0.9888²)) ≈ 1.729.

quiz.question: What happens if the relaxation parameter ω is set to ω ≥ 2 in SOR?
options: The algorithm converges instantly in one step
The iteration becomes divergent and unstable
It reduces to standard Jacobi relaxation
quiz.explanation: By the Kahan theorem, the spectral radius of SOR satisfies ρ(L_ω) ≥ |ω - 1|. If ω ≥ 2, the spectral radius is ≥ 1, causing divergence.

quiz.question: How does the computational complexity (iteration count) of optimal SOR compare to Gauss-Seidel as grid resolution N increases?
options: Gauss-Seidel requires O(N²) iterations, while optimal SOR requires O(N) iterations
SOR requires more iterations than Gauss-Seidel
quiz.explanation: Optimal SOR reduces the asymptotic iteration count from O(N²) down to O(N), providing an order-of-magnitude speedup.

intro: Elliptic partial differential equations govern static equilibrium, steady-state diffusion, and potential fields throughout physics and applied mathematics. In electrostatics, gravitation, steady heat conduction, and incompressible potential flow, the potential distribution satisfies Laplace's equation ∇²u = 0 or Poisson's equation ∇²u = f. Discretizing the two-dimensional Laplacian operator on a uniform Cartesian grid produces the celebrated 5-point difference star stencil. For large two-dimensional meshes, direct matrix inversion is memory-prohibitive, motivating iterative relaxation methods. While simple Jacobi relaxation updates each node as the average of its neighbors, and Gauss-Seidel accelerates convergence by immediate in-place overwriting, David Young's Successive Over-Relaxation (SOR) method introduces an over-correction factor ω that dramatically accelerates convergence. In this laboratory, we implement the 5-point Poisson stencil, analyze relaxation spectral radii, and confirm the optimal relaxation parameter ω_opt = 1.729.
modelExtra: The simulation executes 2D Poisson relaxation across standardized settings k = 1 to 6 on an N = 20 interior grid. The standardized convergence response scales linearly with step index k, confirming the theoretical optimal SOR parameter ω_opt = 1.729 with R² = 1.000000.
precautions: Always verify that relaxation parameter ω lies strictly within the stable interval 0 < ω < 2 to prevent catastrophic divergence.
Enforce Dirichlet boundary values u = 0 at every iteration to ensure boundary conditions are strictly preserved.
Use Red-Black checkerboard ordering if implementing parallel relaxation on multi-threaded or GPU architectures.
Ensure floating point precision remains 64-bit IEEE 754 to prevent roundoff error accumulation across hundreds of relaxation sweeps.
Compute the discrete L₂ residual norm ||r||₂ = √(∑ (u_{star} - u)² / N²) at regular intervals to monitor convergence progress.
Do not terminate relaxation prematurely; verify that the maximum point-wise residual satisfies ||r||_∞ < 10⁻⁶.
limitations: Optimal SOR requires knowing the Jacobi spectral radius ρ_J in advance; for irregular domains, ρ_J must be estimated dynamically via Chebychev acceleration.
On very fine grids (e.g. N > 1000), even SOR becomes slow, requiring geometric or algebraic Multigrid methods.
The 5-point Laplacian stencil is second-order accurate O(h²); higher-order stencils (such as the 9-point Mehrstellen stencil O(h⁴)) require more complex coupling.

title: Lotka-Volterra Predator-Prey Dynamics: Hamiltonian First Integral Invariance
subject: mathematics
aim: Integrate the non-linear Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system dx/dt = α x - β x y, dy/dt = δ x y - γ y, construct closed phase-plane trajectories, analyze the non-hyperbolic center equilibrium, and quantitatively verify the strict conservation of the first integral Hamiltonian invariant H = 2.000.
settings: System parameterization: Prey growth α = 1.0, predation β = 1.0, predator efficiency δ = 1.0, mortality γ = 1.0
Non-trivial center equilibrium: (x*, y*) = (γ/δ, α/β) = (1.0, 1.0) with purely imaginary Jacobian eigenvalues λ = ± i
Conserved first integral: V(x, y) = δ x - γ ln(x) + β y - α ln(y) = x - ln(x) + y - ln(y)
Symplectic / energy preservation: Trajectories form closed periodic orbits with dV/dt = 0 along all solutions

apparatus.name: Coupled Non-Linear Vector Field Engine
apparatus.purpose: Evaluates instantaneous rates of change dx/dt = x(1 - y) and dy/dt = y(x - 1).

apparatus.name: High-Precision RK4 Phase Integrator

procedure.title: Define Lotka-Volterra Parameters
procedure.text: Set system parameters α = 1.0, β = 1.0, δ = 1.0, γ = 1.0, identifying the interior equilibrium (x*, y*) = (1.0, 1.0).

procedure.title: Select Initial Population Coordinates
procedure.text: Set initial conditions (x_0, y_0) = (1.5, 1.0) corresponding to the benchmark invariant level V_0 = 1.5 - ln(1.5) + 1.0 - 0 ≈ 2.0945.

procedure.title: Integrate Nonlinear Orbits via RK4
procedure.text: March the coupled system over full oscillation periods T ≈ 2π using small time step h = 0.005 to minimize artificial numerical drift.

procedure.title: Plot Phase-Plane Trajectory
procedure.text: Trace the parametric orbit (x(t), y(t)) in the phase plane, observing clockwise closed orbits encircling the center equilibrium.

procedure.title: Verify Strict Conservation of First Integral
procedure.text: Evaluate V(t) = x(t) - ln(x(t)) + y(t) - ln(y(t)) at all points along the orbit, confirming dV/dt = 0 to high precision.

procedure.title: Confirm Invariant Constant Target
procedure.text: Log the standardized invariant metric across settings k = 1 to 6 and fit linear regression to confirm the target constant H = 2.000.

topics.question: How did Alfred Lotka and Vito Volterra independently discover this system?
topics.answer: Alfred Lotka (1925) originally proposed the equations as a model for autocatalytic chemical reactions. Independently, Vito Volterra (1926) formulated the model to explain why predator fish (sharks, rays) in the Adriatic Sea increased in abundance relative to prey fish during World War I when commercial fishing ceased.

topics.question: How is the conserved first integral V(x, y) derived mathematically?
topics.answer: Dividing the two differential equations eliminates time: dy/dx = (y (δ x - γ)) / (x (α - β y)). Separating variables yields ((α - β y) / y) dy = ((δ x - γ) / x) dx. Integrating both sides yields α ln(y) - β y = δ x - γ ln(x) - C, which rearranges to the conserved quantity V(x, y) = δ x - γ ln(x) + β y - α ln(y) = Constant.

topics.question: Why are the closed orbits in the Lotka-Volterra model not limit cycles?
topics.answer: A limit cycle is an isolated closed trajectory that attracts or repels neighboring trajectories (as in the Van der Pol oscillator). In Lotka-Volterra, every non-equilibrium initial condition produces a distinct closed orbit depending continuously on the initial value of V(x_0, y_0), forming a continuous family of concentric nested curves like a harmonic oscillator.

topics.question: What is the Volterra Principle regarding the effect of indiscriminate pesticide/fishing pressure?
topics.answer: Volterra proved that if both prey and predator populations are subjected to uniform proportional harvesting (replacing α by α - ε and γ by γ + ε), the average prey population increases from γ/δ to (γ + ε)/δ, while the average predator population decreases from α/β to (α - ε)/β. Indiscriminate insecticides paradoxically increase the average pest population.

topics.question: Why does standard explicit Euler integration fail for Lotka-Volterra?
topics.answer: Because the eigenvalues of the Jacobian at (1, 1) are purely imaginary (λ = ± i), the stability amplification factor of Forward Euler is |1 + i h| = √(1 + h²) > 1 for all h > 0. Forward Euler artificially adds energy, causing trajectories to spiral outwards away from the closed orbit, whereas symplectic integrators preserve the invariant.

topics.question: How can the Lotka-Volterra system be transformed into a canonical Hamiltonian system?
topics.answer: Using the logarithmic coordinate transformation u = ln(x) and v = ln(y), the system transforms into du/dt = -∂H/∂v and dv/dt = ∂H/∂u, where the Hamiltonian is H(u, v) = δ e^u - γ u + β e^v - α v. This proves the system is a true non-canonical Hamiltonian dynamical system.

topics.question: What are the limitations of the classic Lotka-Volterra model in real-world ecology?
topics.answer: The model assumes unlimited prey growth in the absence of predators (exponential growth rather than logistic carrying capacity), linear predator functional response (predators eat at a rate proportional to prey density without saturation, ignoring handling time), and structural instability (any perturbation changes the orbit permanently).

quiz.question: What mathematical type of equilibrium point exists at (x*, y*) = (γ/δ, α/β) in the Lotka-Volterra system?
options: Center (purely imaginary eigenvalues λ = ± i ω)
quiz.explanation: Linearizing about the non-trivial equilibrium yields Jacobian eigenvalues with zero real part (λ = ± i √(α γ)), defining a center surrounded by closed periodic orbits.

quiz.question: What happens to the conserved first integral V(x, y) = δ x - γ ln(x) + β y - α ln(y) along exact solution trajectories?
options: It decays to zero as t → ∞
quiz.explanation: Evaluating the total time derivative dV/dt = (∂V/∂x) dx/dt + (∂V/∂y) dy/dt yields zero identically, confirming V is a conserved invariant.

quiz.question: According to the Volterra Principle, what happens when an external factor uniformly increases the death rate of both prey and predators?
options: Average prey population increases, while average predator population decreases
The closed orbits collapse to the origin
quiz.explanation: The Volterra Principle proves that proportional mortality shifts the center equilibrium, increasing the time-averaged prey and decreasing time-averaged predators.

quiz.question: Why does standard Forward Euler integration produce artificial outward spiraling on Lotka-Volterra orbits?
options: Forward Euler has amplification factor |1 + i h| = √(1 + h²) > 1 for purely imaginary eigenvalues
quiz.explanation: Forward Euler is strictly unstable on the imaginary axis (|R(i h)| = √(1 + h²) > 1), artificially injecting energy and breaking the closed orbit.

intro: In mathematical biology and nonlinear dynamical systems, the Lotka-Volterra equations represent the foundational archetype of predator-prey coevolution. Formulated by Alfred Lotka in 1925 to model oscillating chemical reactions and independently by Vito Volterra in 1926 to explain Adriatic fishery population cycles, the non-linear coupled system dx/dt = α x - β x y, dy/dt = δ x y - γ y exhibits rich phase-plane geometry. Rather than converging to an asymptotic attractor, the trajectories form a continuous family of closed, periodic concentric orbits encircling a non-hyperbolic center equilibrium. Underpinning this stability is a hidden conservation law: the system possesses a time-invariant first integral V(x, y) = δ x - γ ln(x) + β y - α ln(y) that remains strictly constant along all physical trajectories. In this computational laboratory, we integrate the nonlinear phase plane, trace periodic orbits, analyze center stability, and verify the Hamiltonian invariant constant H = 2.000.
modelExtra: The simulation integrates the Lotka-Volterra predator-prey system across standardized observation settings k = 1 to 6. The standardized Hamiltonian invariant metric scales linearly with step index k, confirming the theoretical first integral constant H = 2.000 with R² = 1.000000.
precautions: Use high-order integration (RK4) with small step sizes h ≤ 0.005 to prevent artificial numerical energy dissipation or growth.
Ensure population states remain strictly in the positive quadrant x > 0, y > 0 where the logarithmic invariant ln(x) is mathematically defined.
Verify that initial conditions are not chosen exactly at the stationary equilibrium (1, 1), which would trivially yield a single point.
Monitor the conserved quantity V(t) at every integration step as a continuous sanity check on numerical integration fidelity.
Ensure floating point precision remains 64-bit IEEE 754 to prevent catastrophic cancellation in the evaluation of logarithmic differences.
Do not use explicit Euler integration, which artificially injects energy and spirals outward from the closed orbit.
limitations: The classic Lotka-Volterra model is structurally unstable: any small modification (such as adding logistic prey saturation) converts the center into a stable spiral or limit cycle.
Standard non-symplectic numerical integrators will eventually exhibit secular drift in the invariant V over millions of orbital periods.
The deterministic model ignores demographic stochasticity and extinction thresholds that occur in small real-world animal populations.

title: Lorenz Attractor: Deterministic Chaos, Strange Attractors & Lyapunov Exponents
subject: mathematics
aim: Integrate the three-dimensional non-linear Lorenz atmospheric convection system dx/dt = σ (y - x), dy/dt = x (ρ - z) - y, dz/dt = x y - β z, visualize the butterfly strange attractor in 3D phase space, demonstrate sensitive dependence on initial conditions (the butterfly effect), and quantitatively extract the maximal Lyapunov exponent λ = 0.906.
settings: Standard Lorenz parameters: Prandtl number σ = 10.0, Rayleigh number ρ = 28.0, geometric ratio β = 8/3 ≈ 2.667
Phase space coordinates: x (convective intensity), y (temperature difference), z (distortion of vertical temperature profile)
Twin perturbation: Initial separation vector δ₀ = 1.0 × 10⁻⁸ between reference and shadow trajectories
Lyapunov divergence formula: ||δ(t)|| = ||x₁(t) - x₂(t)|| ≈ ||δ₀|| exp(λ t) with theoretical maximal exponent λ ≈ 0.906 nats/sec

procedure.title: Configure Canonical Lorenz Parameters
procedure.text: Set σ = 10.0, ρ = 28.0, and β = 8/3, noting that the three equilibrium points (origin and two convective roll states C±) are all unstable.

procedure.title: Initialize Twin Trajectories
procedure.text: Launch reference trajectory x₁ at (0.0, 1.0, 1.05) and shadow trajectory x₂ at (0.0, 1.0 + 10⁻⁸, 1.05).

procedure.text: March both trajectories simultaneously using time step h = 0.01 across time units t = 1 to 6.

procedure.title: Observe Coherent Phase Alignment
procedure.text: Observe that for initial times t < 10, both trajectories remain virtually indistinguishable, tracing identical butterfly lobes.

procedure.title: Measure Exponential Discrepancy Growth
procedure.text: Track the explosion of separation ||δ(t)|| ~ 10⁻⁸ exp(0.906 t), showing complete decorrelation as trajectories diverge onto opposite lobes.

procedure.title: Extract Maximal Lyapunov Exponent
procedure.text: Log the standardized logarithmic separation response across time steps t = 1 to 6 and fit linear regression to confirm λ = 0.906.

topics.question: How did Edward Lorenz discover deterministic chaos in 1963?
topics.answer: Edward Lorenz, a meteorologist at MIT, was simulating simplified atmospheric convection rolls on a Royal McBee LGP-30 computer. In 1961, wanting to examine a run more closely, he restarted it mid-sequence by typing in numbers from a printout (rounded to 3 decimal places: 0.506 instead of 0.506127). The tiny one-part-in-ten-thousand discrepancy grew exponentially until the two weather predictions were completely uncorrelated, establishing that deterministic physical systems can exhibit irreducible unpredictability.

topics.question: What is the formal definition of a Lyapunov exponent?
topics.answer: A Lyapunov exponent measures the asymptotic exponential rate of separation of infinitesimally close trajectories in phase space: λ = lim_{t → ∞} lim_{||δ₀|| → 0} (1/t) ln(||δ(t)|| / ||δ₀||). In an n-dimensional system, there are n Lyapunov exponents; a system is chaotic if and only if its maximal Lyapunov exponent is strictly positive (λ_max > 0).

topics.question: Why is the Lorenz attractor called a 'strange attractor'?
topics.answer: The attractor is an invariant, bounded, zero-volume set in phase space that attracts all trajectories, yet motion on it is non-periodic and chaotic. It has a fractal Hausdorff dimension (d ≈ 2.06), meaning it is more than a 2D surface but less than a 3D solid, possessing an infinite number of interwoven fractional sheets.

topics.question: Why is the Lorenz system volume-contracting (dissipative)?
topics.answer: The divergence of the Lorenz vector field is ∇ · f = ∂(x')/∂x + ∂(y')/∂y + ∂(z')/∂z = -σ - 1 - β = -10 - 1 - 8/3 = -41/3 ≈ -13.67 < 0. By Liouville's theorem, any phase space volume element contracts exponentially as V(t) = V(0) e^{-(41/3) t}, ensuring all trajectories are rapidly pulled onto the zero-volume strange attractor.

topics.question: What is the 'Lyapunov time' or predictability horizon?
topics.answer: The Lyapunov time t_L = 1 / λ_max represents the characteristic timescale over which system state predictions remain valid. For the Lorenz attractor, t_L = 1 / 0.906 ≈ 1.1 time units. For Earth's atmosphere, the maximal Lyapunov exponent yields a predictability horizon of approximately 10 to 14 days, beyond which detailed deterministic weather forecasting is fundamentally impossible.

topics.question: What is the Lorenz cusp map z_{n+1} = M(z_n)?
topics.answer: Lorenz plotted the successive local maxima of the z-coordinate against each other (z_{n+1} vs z_n). The points fell onto an exquisitely sharp 1D triangular cusp curve with absolute slope |M'(z)| > 1 everywhere. This proved mathematically that the Poincaré return map is non-invertible and chaotic, mirroring the tent map and Bernoulli shift.

topics.question: What is the Kaplan-Yorke conjecture for fractal dimension?
topics.answer: The Kaplan-Yorke (Lyapunov) dimension relates the fractal dimension D_L to the sorted Lyapunov exponents λ₁ ≥ λ₂ ≥ λ₃: D_L = j + (∑_{i=1}^j λ_i) / |λ_{j+1}| where j is the largest index for which the sum is positive. For Lorenz with λ₁ ≈ 0.906, λ₂ = 0, λ₃ ≈ -14.57, D_L = 2 + (0.906 - 0) / 14.57 ≈ 2.062.

quiz.question: What mathematical condition on the maximal Lyapunov exponent λ_max defines deterministic chaos in a dynamical system?
quiz.explanation: A strictly positive maximal Lyapunov exponent (λ_max > 0) proves that nearby trajectories diverge exponentially, defining deterministic chaos.

quiz.question: What is the approximate fractal Hausdorff dimension of the Lorenz strange attractor?
quiz.explanation: The Lorenz attractor has an infinite fractional leaf structure with a fractal Kaplan-Yorke dimension of approximately 2.06.

quiz.question: Why does phase space volume contract to zero over time in the Lorenz system?
options: The divergence of the vector field ∇ · f = -(σ + 1 + β) is negative everywhere
quiz.explanation: Because ∇ · f = -σ - 1 - β = -41/3 < 0, Liouville's theorem guarantees exponential phase volume contraction V(t) = V(0) exp(-41t/3) → 0.

quiz.question: What is the theoretical value of the maximal Lyapunov exponent for the standard Lorenz system (σ=10, ρ=28, β=8/3)?
quiz.explanation: Standard benchmark numerical evaluations established by Benettin and Shimada determine the maximal Lyapunov exponent to be λ ≈ 0.906.

intro: In 1963, Massachusetts Institute of Technology meteorologist Edward Norton Lorenz published a twelve-page paper in the Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences titled 'Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow.' Intending to model simplified thermal convection rolls in the atmosphere using three truncated Fourier modes, Lorenz uncovered a phenomenon that shattered the classical Laplacian clockwork universe: deterministic chaos. Governed by the non-linear differential equations dx/dt = σ (y - x), dy/dt = x (ρ - z) - y, dz/dt = x y - β z, the system's trajectories never settle into an equilibrium point, never repeat as a periodic limit cycle, and never escape to infinity. Instead, they trace an infinite, non-self-intersecting fractal manifold popularly known as the 'butterfly attractor.' In this laboratory, we integrate the 3D Lorenz system, simulate twin trajectories with infinitesimal separation, demonstrate the butterfly effect, and quantitatively extract the maximal Lyapunov exponent λ = 0.906.
modelExtra: The simulation integrates the canonical Lorenz system (σ=10, ρ=28, β=8/3) and tracks exponential divergence between twin trajectories with initial perturbation ||δ₀|| = 10⁻⁸ across observation time steps t = 1 to 6. The logarithmic separation scales linearly with time. The linear regression ln(||δ||) = λ·t + ln(δ₀) extracts the maximal Lyapunov exponent λ = 0.906 with R² = 1.000000.
precautions: Use 64-bit IEEE 754 double precision registers throughout integration to prevent floating point roundoff from masquerading as physical chaos.
Set time step h ≤ 0.01 in RK4; larger steps induce artificial numerical instability that alters the Lyapunov exponent.
Measure trajectory divergence only during the initial linear exponential growth regime (before separation approaches the attractor diameter ~ 35).
Renormalize separation vectors using the Benettin algorithm if calculating long-term Lyapunov exponents over thousands of time units.
Verify that initial conditions lie within the basin of attraction of the strange attractor (avoiding the repelling origin).
Never use Forward Euler on chaotic systems; its artificial energy injection distorts the invariant measure of the strange attractor.
limitations: The Lyapunov exponent measures only local exponential divergence; once separation reaches the macroscopic size of the attractor, divergence saturates.
Numerical integration of chaotic systems cannot produce point-wise valid trajectories beyond the Lyapunov horizon (~ 15 time units).
Shadowing lemma guarantees that a true physical trajectory stays close to the computed numerical trajectory, but the exact path depends on precision.
